title: How to Quiet a Noisy Return-Air Vent or Rattling Register
question: Why is my return air vent so loud, and how do I make it quieter?
summary: A loud return vent is usually air moving too fast through too small an opening, made worse by a dirty or very dense filter. A rattle or buzz is different: that is loose metal shaking. Start with a clean filter and open supply vents, then quiet the grille, then fit a larger grille with more open area. A lined duct or baffle behind the grille can cut blower noise, but never block or shrink the return.

commonCauses.cause: A dirty or too-dense filter. A clogged filter, or a high-MERV filter squeezed into a thin 1-inch slot, adds resistance. The blower pulls harder and the return roars or whistles.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Pull the filter and hold it up to a light. If you cannot see light through it, replace it. Check the MERV number on the frame. In one set of tests, a MERV 11 filter had about three times the pressure drop of a basic MERV 2 filter.

commonCauses.cause: The return grille or duct is too small for the airflow. Many homes have one central return sized too tight. Air rushes through the grille fast, and fast air is loud. Padding the grille will not fix this.
commonCauses.quickCheck: With the blower running, hold a tissue near the grille. If it snaps flat and the sound is a steady roar that does not change when you press on the grille, the opening is too small.

commonCauses.cause: A loose grille, louvers, or thin duct. The metal grille, its blades, or a flat panel of sheet-metal duct shakes when the blower starts. This is a rattle or buzz, not a roar.
commonCauses.quickCheck: With the system running, press firmly on the grille, then on the duct behind it if you can reach it. If the noise stops or changes, it is vibration.

commonCauses.cause: Closed supply vents or closed doors. Closing supply vents raises the pressure in the whole system. Bedrooms with a supply vent but no return path pressurize when the door is shut, so air whistles under doors and the central return works harder.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Open every supply vent and move rugs and furniture off them. Then compare the noise with the bedroom doors open and shut. If it drops with the doors open, the rooms need a return path.

commonCauses.cause: Blower noise traveling straight out the return. When the return grille sits right next to the furnace or air handler, such as in a hall closet or on the equipment cabinet, blower hum comes straight through with nothing to soften it.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look at where the grille is. If you can almost see the blower through it, or the duct between them is short and straight, the noise is the blower itself.

commonCauses.cause: A gap or a partly closed damper. Air forced through a small gap whistles: a filter door that does not seal, a filter that is the wrong size, or a damper left half shut.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Run the system and move your ear along the grille and duct. A sharp, high whistle from one spot usually means one small gap.

fixes: Put in a clean filter of the exact size. Use the filter type your furnace or air-handler manual lists, often MERV 8 to 11. If you want MERV 13 for cleaner air, use a larger or deeper filter or filter grille so the air moves through it slowly; do not just force a dense filter into a thin slot.

Open every supply vent and keep rugs and furniture off them. Check that dampers on the ducts you can reach are open (a handle in line with the duct is open). Do not close vents in unused rooms. A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory study found that closing registers raised energy use because duct leakage went up.

Find out which noise you have. With the blower running, press on the grille, its blades, and the duct behind it. If pressing stops a buzz or rattle, it is vibration (next step). If you hear a steady roar that pressing does not change, the air is moving too fast (the steps after that).

Stop a rattle. Turn the system off. Remove the grille, stick thin foam weatherstrip or felt tape around the back of its frame, and screw it back until snug without bending it. If the blades chatter, set them fully open and put a small dab of clear silicone at the pivots. If the filter in a filter grille thumps, check that it fits snugly and the latches hold it.

Quiet the roar with more open area. The label or spec sheet of a grille lists its "free area," the open space air can pass through. A bigger grille, or one with a lattice (egg-crate) face instead of stamped louvers, lets the same air move slower and more quietly. Grille makers publish charts of airflow against noise for each size. A central system moves roughly 400 cubic feet per minute per ton of cooling, so a 3-ton system needs a return that stays quiet at about 1,200 cubic feet per minute.

Give closed rooms a way back. If the noise falls when doors are open, ask an HVAC contractor about a transfer grille through the wall, a jumper duct through the ceiling, or a larger door undercut. A 1-inch undercut passes only about 60 cubic feet per minute, which is less than many bedrooms get.

Add a baffle or lined duct for blower noise. What people call an "air return baffle" is a bend or box lined with duct liner between the grille and the blower. It blocks the straight path for sound. The baffle must not shrink the opening, or it makes the roar worse, and it must be built from materials rated for air ducts. Foam, cardboard, and carpet are not. This is usually a job for an HVAC contractor.
Stop a whistle at a gap. Open a half-shut damper fully. Make sure the filter door seats flat and the filter is the right size, so air goes through the filter and not around it.

If it is still loud, have an HVAC contractor measure total external static pressure. Most residential systems are rated for about 0.5 inch of water column, but check your unit's label or manual. A reading well above the rating means the return is too small. The fix is a larger or second return, not a slower blower setting, which can freeze the coil or overheat the furnace.
diyVsPro: You can do most of this yourself: filters, opening vents, gasketing and tightening grilles, quieting blades, and swapping in a larger grille where the opening already fits it. Call an HVAC contractor when a steady roar survives those fixes, when you need a second return, a transfer grille, or a jumper duct cut into walls or ceilings, when you want a lined baffle behind the grille, or when the system needs a static pressure test. Resizing ducts and changing blower speed are jobs for a licensed HVAC technician.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: $0-$40 (filter $10-$25, foam weatherstrip or felt tape $5-$15, silicone $5). Larger return grille or filter grille: $20-$60. HVAC service call with a static pressure test: $90-$200. Adding a return, transfer grille, jumper duct, or lined baffle: $300-$1,200 or more, depending on access.
timeEstimate: 15-30 minutes for a filter, opening vents, and gasketing a grille. 1-2 hours to swap a grille or brace a duct you can reach. Return duct work by a contractor: half a day to a full day.
safetyNote: Before you take off a grille or reach into a return, set the thermostat to off and turn off the furnace or air handler at its service switch so the blower cannot start. Never close off, cover, or stuff anything into a return to quiet it. Starving the system of air can freeze an AC coil and can overheat a gas furnace, which can crack the heat exchanger and let carbon monoxide into the house. Do not open the furnace cabinet or change blower speed yourself: the wiring carries line voltage and the settings are specific to the model. Use a steady ladder for ceiling grilles.
toolsParts: Filter of the exact size and a MERV rating your equipment manual allows
Thin self-adhesive foam weatherstrip or felt tape
Clear silicone sealant for chattering blades
Larger return grille or filter grille with more free area (optional)
Duct mastic or a stiffening strip for a flat duct panel that pops (optional)
Tissue or a strip of paper to judge airflow at the grille
